records.name: Alberta
records.summary:
In December 2024 this province enacted a package of three laws affecting transgender people as a class: school rules requiring parental notification and consent before staff use a student's gender-related chosen name or pronouns; a prohibition on puberty blockers and hormone therapy for minors; and related vital-statistics amendments. Trans and intersex advocacy organisations said at the time they would continue legal action.

In December 2025 the government invoked the constitutional override clause to shield all three laws from judicial remedy. Two national 2SLGBTQ+ organisations, together with five gender-diverse young people, say the constitutional challenge continues despite the shield - a provincial posture of legislating trans-targeting rules and then placing them beyond the courts.

sources.summary: CBC (4 Dec 2024): Alberta's trio of trans-youth bills passed final legislative stage — the Education Amendment Act 2024 (parental opt-in for classroom instruction, student pronoun and sport rules), a health-statutes act barring certain gender-affirming care for minors, plus sports policy. Egale Canada and the Skipping Stone Foundation announced constitutional litigation, calling the package discriminatory.

CBC (Dec 2024): Bill 9, the Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, passed at the tail of the fall sitting, invoking the Charter's notwithstanding clause to shield the three trans-youth laws from legal challenge for years; Egale Canada, Skipping Stone Foundation and five families said their court challenge to Bill 26 continues regardless. Result: laws in force, constitutional litigation pending.

records.name: Saskatchewan
records.summary:
In August 2023 the provincial government announced school policies requiring parents to be asked for permission before staff use a student's preferred name or pronouns (for pupils under 16), parents to be informed about the sexual-health curriculum, and third-party school programs to be paused. The province's senior trial court struck the rule down as unconstitutional; the government responded by legislating the consent rule into the Education Act and invoking the notwithstanding clause to immunise it from judicial review.

The matter went to the province's Court of Appeal, which largely allowed the government's appeal in August 2025; a current-status verification found no later ruling, leaving the re-legislated, shielded policy standing. For a visitor the education rule is primarily resident-facing; the durable signal is institutional: a provincial government re-legislating a policy a court had voided and shielding that from rights review - official hostility hardened past ordinary litigation.

sources.summary: Government of Saskatchewan education-ministry news release (22 Aug 2023) announcing the parental inclusion and consent policies: schools must seek parent/guardian permission before changing the preferred name and pronouns of students under 16, parents must be informed about the sexual-health curriculum, and third-party school programs were paused. The release that started the court challenge.

Saskatchewan (Minister of Education) v UR Pride Centre, 2025 SKCA 74 (11 Aug 2025): the Court of Appeal set aside the 2023 chambers decision — courts lack jurisdiction to test s.1/s.15 Charter breaches of the school pronoun-notice policy where s.33 was invoked — so the policy stands. Supersedes the injunction-era chambers ruling.

The Saskatchewan Court of Appeal ruled Aug. 11, 2025 on the provincial government's appeal in the challenge to the school pronoun law, granting the government's appeal in part but holding that a judge has jurisdiction to determine whether the law limits Charter rights, and that (LGBTQ+ group) UR Pride's litigation may continue in the Court of King's Bench. The 2023 law requires parental consent before children under 16 change their names or pronouns at school, and the government had argued its use of the notwithstanding clause should end the challenge entirely. Egale Canada co-counsel Bennett Jensen said UR Pride will continue the litigation, noting students had been 'living under the reality of this law' for two years. This mainstream coverage independently traces the record's claim that the appeal court largely allowed the government's appeal while keeping the merits challenge alive.

Amnesty International Canada welcomed the Aug. 11, 2025 decision of the Court of Appeal for Saskatchewan as a 'meaningful victory for the protection of human rights in Canada', saying courts can still determine whether the province's anti-trans pronoun law violates the Charter and issue a declaration to that effect even where the notwithstanding clause shields the law from being struck down. Amnesty participated as an intervenor in the appeal, arguing that use of the clause must align with Canada's international-law obligation to provide an effective remedy. The piece corroborates the durable signal this record draws from the case: a consent and name-change rule for transgender pupils shielded from ordinary rights review while litigation continues.

On Nov. 6, 2025 the Supreme Court of Canada said it will hear the appeals in the challenge to Saskatchewan's school pronoun law, which since 2023 has required parental consent before children under 16 change their names or pronouns at school and has been shielded by the province's invocation of the Charter's notwithstanding clause (a five-year override). Both the province and LGBTQ+ group UR Pride appealed the Court of Appeal decision that the challenge can continue, and asked for the hearing to be expedited alongside the challenge to Quebec's Bill 21. The grant is the key later development for this record: no merits ruling has changed the policy, but the constitutionality of the re-legislated, shielded consent rule is now before Canada's highest court.

records.name: New Brunswick
records.summary:
New Brunswick is the clearest Canadian case of a provincial government reversing course on trans rights within one election cycle. Policy 713 (2020) originally protected 2SLGBTQIA+ student privacy and inclusion. In July 2023, the Higgs government amended it to require parental consent for under-16 name/pronoun use, triggering protests outside the legislature. The Holt government reversed the amendment on 19 December 2024, effective 1 January 2025: parental consent is now "encouraged but no longer required" for the informal use of chosen names and pronouns by students of any age (it remains required for formal use in official records for students under 16), with a "presumed capacity" concept based on child-and-youth-advocate recommendations. The revised policy text extends its application to the whole school environment, including "visiting professionals, student teachers, parents, volunteers, and visitors", so current school rules technically reach non-residents present in classrooms.

sources.summary: CBC (19 Dec 2024): the Holt government's revised Policy 713, effective 1 Jan 2025, restores students of any age choosing names and pronouns for informal school use — parental consent 'encouraged' but not required — while formal records for under-16s still need parental consent; it goes beyond child advocate Kelly Lamrock's recommendations and undoes the PCs' 2023 consent rule that drew protests and a CCLA constitutional challenge.

Full text of Policy 713 (Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity), Department of Education and Early Childhood Development, as revised 1 Jan 2025 (effective Aug 17 2020; revised Jul 1/Aug 23 2023 and Jan 1 2025). Its application clause covers the school environment including all students plus "school personnel, contract/casual employees, visiting professionals, student teachers, parents, volunteers, and visitors" — the school-environment rules therefore reach non-residents present in classrooms.

On 1 July 2023, changes to New Brunswick's Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity policy (Policy 713) took effect, barring teachers from using the preferred names and pronouns of students under 16 without parental consent and dropping explicit wording that let students take part in extracurricular activities, including sports teams, reflecting their gender identity. Premier Blaine Higgs's Progressive Conservative government updated the policy without a legislative vote, citing complaints from parents and teachers, and two ministers quit in protest while two others were pushed out. Party dissidents called for a leadership review and Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said trans kids in New Brunswick 'need to feel safe, not targeted by politicians'. Documents the July 2023 amendment and political crisis this record describes.

Canadian Press via Global News (9 June 2023): the Higgs government's proposed Policy 713 changes would force children under 16 to get parental consent to change their names or pronouns at school, with the changes set to take effect 1 July 2023, reversing a three-year-old policy that required teachers to get the student's informed consent before discussing names and pronouns with parents. Eight Progressive Conservative members, including six cabinet ministers, sat out question period to protest the lack of process and transparency, and Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said trans kids in New Brunswick 'need to feel safe, not targeted by politicians'. Confirms the under-16 parental-consent rule, the 1 July effective date, and the caucus revolt behind this record's 2023 amendment.

About 350 people rallied at the New Brunswick legislature on 14 May 2023 to protest the government's review of Policy 713, the 2020 policy that requires schools to respect students' chosen names and pronouns and provide gender-neutral bathrooms. Gail Costello of Pride in Education, who helped write the policy, said 'we know it saves lives' and warned that 'with this policy changed or removed, we're going to lose kids', while Education Minister Bill Hogan confirmed the review. Documents the public protest against the Higgs government's move to amend the sexual-orientation and gender-identity policy this record is about.

records.name: Distrito Federal
records.summary:
The capital recorded the highest transfeminicide toll in the country in 2024 — 17 LGBT+ homicides, of which 11 were trans women — and remains among the highest-count states in 2025. The raw violence data is a negative signal for a visitor, though part of the elevated count reflects the capital's superior reporting infrastructure rather than proportionally higher danger.

Counterbalanced by the strongest institutional response of any Mexican state: transfeminicide was made a distinct crime in July 2024 (“Ley Paola Buenrostro”, the second state to do so); a dedicated Transfeminicide Investigation Unit created in December 2024 covers all violent deaths of trans women; a prosecutor's protocol (Acuerdo FGJCDMX/04/2025) requires feminist-context investigation with immediate-action deadlines; and a new Gender Police launched in August 2025 with 30 patrol units. For a visitor assaulted in the capital there is trained machinery to investigate, where other jurisdictions have none. Modestly above the national score (0.55): the protective and investigative framework is the strongest in M

sources.summary: Annual report (May 2025) by a Mexican LGBT+ news collective on homicides of LGBT+ people in Mexico in 2024: for the first time CDMX topped the national count with 17 homicides, 11 of them trans women, ahead of Nuevo León (5); 115 recorded violent incidents nationally, of which 59 killings. The primary state-by-state violence data.

NOTE: cached page returned only site navigation; the underlying CNN en Español report (19 July 2024) covers Mexico City's congress approving transfeminicide as a distinct crime in the penal code — the reform dubbed the "Ley Paola Buenrostro" after a trans woman murdered in 2016, making CDMX the second state to create the offence.

Proceso (20 Dec 2024): CDMX created a dedicated Transfeminicide Investigation Unit; its investigators may no longer demand legal name/gender change or medical documentation from trans people. Context: on 18 Jul 2024 CDMX became the country's second entity to typify transfeminicidio, after the local congress passed the 'Paola Buenrostro' law (named for a trans woman murdered in 2016).

CDMX instrument FGJCDMX/04/2025: article 148-Ter was added to the local code on 23 Aug 2024 typifying transfeminicidio — killing of a trans woman or feminine-spectrum person by reason of gender identity or expression — and the agreement sets initial-response protocol rules for such cases alongside feminicide investigations.

NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (404); the underlying Proceso report (25 Aug 2025) covers the mayor of Mexico City launching the new Gender Police with 30 patrol units to handle cases of violence against women and girls in the capital.

records.name: Nuevo Leon
records.summary:
Three trans women murdered in less than a week in July 2024 (one disappeared and found dead days later; one killed while sex work); four transfeminicides recorded in July 2024 alone and five for the year in the national NGO yearbook — second only to Mexico City. Activists reported six trans women killed in a short period and accused three levels of government of rights omissions. Nuevo León's penal code contains no transfeminicide offence, and its 2019 hate-crime provision covers sexual orientation but not gender identity — meaning a visitor assaulted in Monterrey faces a legal framework with no specific protective category. The state has an anti-conversion-practices law carrying 2-5 years, and the national observatory's verdict on such statutes is that transfeminicide 'advances in law but not in sentences.'

Legislative response has been refusal: an initiative filed by Colectivo Casa Trans was 'ignored and finally lapsed,' prompting a 50+-day protest encampment outside the state congress still ongoing in January 2026 (activists report harassment and lack of basic facilities

sources.summary: Agencia Presentes (31 Jul 2024): three trans women killed in Nuevo Leon in under a week — Arantza Castillo, 23, killed while doing sex work, and a 27 Jun motel victim still unidentified; the state justice ministry issued no case information. Nationally at least 36 trans women were transfemicided in 2024 (Asamblea Nacional Trans No Binarie); at least four in Nuevo Leon that year.

Letra S 'Las dinámicas de la violencia por prejuicio — Homicidios de personas LGBT+ en México, 2024' (May 2025): the country's longest-running civil-society hate-crime observatory (since 1998) yearbook. Records CDMX as the state with the most LGBT+ killings in 2024 (17 homicides, 11 trans women) ahead of Nuevo León (5); notes the Mexican state has no official registry of bias-motivated violence, and documents under-counting where media accounts lack victim names and gender data.

Verificado (2024): Nuevo Leon recorded 7 attacks on LGBT people, 3 forced disappearances and 4 transfeminicides during the year, and transfeminicidio is not typified in the state penal code. A labour diagnostic survey found 42.2% of the state's trans population unemployed and 35.1% discriminated against at work.

ABC Noticias (12 Jan 2026): Colectivo Casa Trans has held a planton of more than 50 days outside the Nuevo Leon congress pressing legislators to typify transfeminicidio in the state penal code; their bill was ignored for a year and lapsed, forcing a fresh filing.

records.name: Michoacan de Ocampo
records.summary:
The state has not typified hate crime at all, per its own LGBT+ welfare sub-director (June 2026), who also located most attacks on the community in Tierra Caliente, the zone of armed-group influence. Six LGBT+ homicides were recorded in the first four and a half months of 2026 alone, including 'Daniela,' a trans woman found beaten to death in a drainage channel in Morelia on 2 April 2026 — a suspect was arrested, a positive institutional response. Two additional deaths in Morelia in April 2026, one of them a gay man, were linked by the attorney general's office to organised crime. An NGO observatory report counted 46 LGBT+ homicides in Michoacán between 2015 and 2024, led by Morelia (11), then Lázaro Cárdenas (6), Apatzingán and Uruapan (5) and Zamora (4), with 2015 the deadliest year (10 victims).

sources.summary: El Sol de Morelia (OEM; body partly navigation-only): the majority of attacks on the LGBT community in Michoacan concentrate in Tierra Caliente, and the state has not typified the murder of sexual-diversity people as a hate crime (the article's own standfirst).

NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (La Jornada blocks automated fetch); the underlying article (15 Apr 2026) reports the arrest of a suspect in the killing of 'Daniela', a trans woman found beaten to death in a drainage channel in Morelia (2 Apr 2026), and counts six LGBT+ homicides in the state in the first four and a half months of 2026.

Quadratín Michoacán (16 May 2025) reports the Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes contra Personas LGBT count for the state: 46 LGBT+ homicides in Michoacán between 2015 and 2024, with Morelia highest at 11, followed by Lázaro Cárdenas (6), Apatzingán and Uruapan (5 each) and Zamora (4), and 2015 the deadliest year with 10 victims, presented at a press conference by Raúl Martínez of Colectivo Michoacán es Diversidad. Trans women were the most affected group (27 of the homicides) and people aged 25-39 the most affected age bracket, with 13 disappearances of LGBT+ people reported between 2022 and 2024. Matches the observatory counts cited in this record's summary.

Quadratín Michoacán (16 June 2026) reports that trans women were 58.3% of LGBT+ homicide victims nationally in 2025 (35 of 60 recorded by the Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio contra Personas LGBT+), then gives the Michoacán picture: six homicide cases identified by civil-society groups in the state in 2026 (three in Morelia, one each in Uruapan, Ocampo and Maravatío) and at least 56 registered aggressions against the community since 2014, per Raúl Martínez, spokesperson of Colectivo Michoacán es Diversidad, speaking before the march for the transfeminicide of Daniela. Confirms the ongoing lethal violence against trans women in Michoacán that this record documents.

MiMorelia (11 June 2025) quotes Raúl Martínez of Colectivo Michoacán es Diversidad and the Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio contra Personas LGBT: of the 46 hate-crime cases recorded by civil society in Michoacán since 2015, only one was being processed for judicialization — the murder of Meredith Escarlet, a trans woman killed in Tarímbaro — while the state prosecutor's office keeps no disaggregated data. Martínez said Michoacán has stopped attending to victims and does not recognize the violence, that institutions such as the victims commission, the state human-rights commission and the state council against discrimination lack the capacity or budget to act, and that no public prevention policy exists. Documents the impunity and lack of institutional response central to this record's Michoacán assessment.
